Most people estimate monthly savings interest as balance × APY ÷ 12. It's close, but a little too high, because APY already includes compounding.

Here's the more accurate formula, plus why your first payment often looks small 🧵

The formula:
interest = balance × [(1 + APY)^(days ÷ 365) − 1]

Hypothetical example: $10,000 at 4.00% APY
• 30 days ≈ $32.29
• 31 days ≈ $33.37
• ÷12 shortcut = $33.33

Why the number of days matters: most high-yield accounts compound interest daily and credit it monthly. So a 31-day statement period pays a bit more than a 30-day one or February. Use the exact days between your statement dates.

First interest payment tiny? That's usually normal. Common causes:
• Your money was in the account for only part of the period
• The deposit took a few days to clear
• The statement cycle doesn't follow the calendar month

Rate changed mid-period? Split the period at the change date, work out each part at its own APY and add them together.

Off by a few cents? That's rounding. Bigger gap? Check deposit clear dates, balance tiers and 360- vs 365-day basis.

reddit_title: How to actually calculate your HYSA's monthly interest (and why APY ÷ 12 is slightly off)
reddit_post:
I see a lot of "my interest doesn't match what I expected" posts, so here's how to check it yourself.

**The formula**

interest = balance × [(1 + APY)^(days ÷ 365) − 1]

Use the exact number of days in your statement period (28, 29, 30 or 31, or whatever your cycle is). Don't use "1/12 of a year."

**Example (hypothetical numbers)**

$10,000 at 4.00% APY:
- 30 days: 10,000 × (1.04^(30/365) − 1) ≈ **$32.29**
- 31 days: ≈ **$33.37**
- The APY ÷ 12 shortcut gives $33.33 every month. That's slightly high, because the APY already includes a full year of compounding.

Spreadsheet: `=Balance*((1+APY)^(Days/365)-1)`

**Step by step**

1. **Find your APY** on the bank's rate page or in the interest disclosure. Convert it to a decimal (4.00% = 0.04).
2. **Check how interest is compounded and credited.** Most HYSAs compound daily and credit monthly, but confirm this in your disclosure. Also check whether the bank uses a 365-day or 360-day year.
3. **Count the days** between the statement's start and end dates. If you opened the account partway through, count only the days your money was actually earning interest.
4. **Work out the balance that earned interest.** If you deposited or withdrew money during the period, use the average daily balance. Many statements show it. Otherwise, add up each day's closing balance and divide by the number of days.
5. **Apply the formula.**
6. **If the rate changed mid-period**, split the period at the date the new rate took effect, calculate each part at its own APY and add them together.
7. **Compare with the "interest paid" line on your statement.**

**APY vs. interest rate**

APY includes compounding. The plain interest rate (often loosely called APR) doesn't, so it's a little lower. Use APY to estimate what you'll earn and to compare accounts. Use the interest rate if you want to work out a daily rate.

**"Why was my first payment so small?"**

Usually it's one of these:
- Your money was in the account for only part of the first period
- The deposit took a few days to clear before it started earning
- The statement cycle doesn't follow the calendar month
- Balance tiers or promo-rate conditions

**When to ask the bank**

A difference of a few cents is rounding. If the gap is bigger, check when your deposits cleared, when the rate changed, any balance tiers and the day-count basis. If it still doesn't add up, contact the bank and show them your calculation.

Also, in many countries savings interest counts as taxable income. Check your local rules.
